flashcards.q: What is a feature flag?
flashcards.a: A condition in the code whose on/off state comes from config or data, so you can change it without changing code or deploying.
flashcards.more: The new code is already on the server, switched off. You can open it slowly, and shut it off at once if it goes wrong. It works like a house switchboard: running the wire and turning the switch on are separate acts.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between deploy and release?
flashcards.a: Deploy: the code reaches the server. Release: users can see the feature. A flag separates the two.
flashcards.more: Once they are separate, deploying becomes low-risk because the new code is switched off. The risk moves to the release, which you can do slowly, by percentage, and undo with one switch.

flashcards.q: What are the four kinds of feature flag?
flashcards.a: Release (open slowly), ops/kill switch (emergency off), experiment (A/B) and permission (who gets it).
flashcards.more: The kind decides the lifespan and the owner. Release and experiment flags are temporary: delete them when the job is done. A kill switch lives long, ideally with a runbook. A permission flag is really a business rule, so think of it as part of authorization.

flashcards.q: What is a kill switch and why do you need one?
flashcards.a: A flag that turns off a feature or dependency in an emergency without a deploy, for example a slow payment gateway.
flashcards.more: While it is off, the app must keep working on a fallback path, such as a "this method isn't available right now" message. Keep it where the on-call engineer can find and change it in a minute, and write a runbook for it.

flashcards.q: In a percentage rollout, how do you decide who gets the new feature?
flashcards.a: Hash the user id with the flag name into 0–99. If the number is below the percentage, the feature is on.
flashcards.more: For example, `crc32($name.':'.$userId) % 100 < $percent`. The same id always gets the same number, so once a user has the feature they keep it as you go from 25% to 100%. With random(), they would see the new path one moment and the old one the next.

flashcards.q: Why keep flag state in the database rather than a config file?
flashcards.a: Changing a file needs a deploy; changing a database value doesn't. So you can switch a feature off immediately after a mistake.
flashcards.more: Read it from the database and cache it with a short TTL (say 30 seconds), so you don't hit the database on every request and changes still spread quickly. If the flag can't be found, the default is false.

flashcards.q: What is flag debt and how do you avoid it?
flashcards.a: Finished flags left in the code. Avoid it by giving every flag an owner and a removal date.
flashcards.more: Old flags keep two paths alive, double your tests, and bring back a broken path if someone flips them by mistake. Once a feature hits 100%, remove the flag and the old code within a week. That is part of the release.

flashcards.q: Is hiding a button in Vue with a flag enough to protect a feature?
flashcards.a: No. A user can call the API directly, so the server must block it with the same flag.
flashcards.more: Vue only shows or hides things. The server makes the decision and sends the per-user result (true/false) through an API. The client never needs to know the percentage or the allow list.

flashcards.q: How do you make sure finished release flags actually get removed?
flashcards.a: Record an owner and a remove_by date for each flag in a registry, and add a CI test that fails once a release flag is overdue.
flashcards.more: A red build on the due date names the flag, so nobody has to remember. If the date truly can't be met, move it in a reviewed commit rather than skipping the test. Ops flags (kill switches) have no remove_by.

flashcards.q: What is config, and where should it live?
flashcards.a: Whatever changes between environments (addresses, timeouts, keys). Keep it outside the code, in environment variables or secrets.
flashcards.more: The code stays the same and the values change. If you put values in the code, you have to change the code for every environment, and passwords end up in git. The code is the recipe; the config is the separate slip with the ingredient amounts.

flashcards.q: What does the 12-factor rule say about config?
flashcards.a: Keep config in environment variables. One build runs in every environment, and the differences come from outside values.
flashcards.more: What you tested on staging is exactly what ships to prod. Changing config doesn't need a new build. There are no secrets in the image, so it does no harm if the image spreads.

flashcards.q: In Symfony, what is the difference between .env and .env.local?
flashcards.a: .env is committed to git and holds safe defaults. .env.local stays out of git and holds values for your own machine.
flashcards.more: Real environment variables on the server always win over .env files. In production you normally use the server's env or secrets rather than .env.local. To check, run `php bin/console debug:dotenv`.

flashcards.q: Env variables are always strings. How do you get a number or a bool?
flashcards.a: With env processors: %env(int:NAME)% or #[Autowire(env: 'bool:NAME')].
flashcards.more: There are processors such as `int:`, `bool:`, `float:`, `json:`, `file:` and `default:`. They convert the type as the value is read, so you don't get type errors later. Without one, the string "5" arrives and can cause odd behavior.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between config and a secret?
flashcards.a: Leaking config (a timeout, a URL) does little harm; leaking a secret (a password, an API key) does. Secrets live somewhere separate and safe.
flashcards.more: Config can sit in .env in git as safe defaults. Secrets go in the Symfony secrets vault or a cloud secret manager. A key that reached git by mistake can't be fixed by deleting it: it stays in git history, so you have to rotate the key.

flashcards.q: How does the Symfony secrets vault work?
flashcards.a: secrets:set encrypts a value. The encrypted file goes into git, while the decrypt key reaches the server separately.
flashcards.more: The encrypt (public) key and the encrypted values live in the repository. The prod decrypt (private) key never goes into git; in production it is supplied through the `SYMFONY_DECRYPTION_SECRET` env variable or a separate file. Dev and prod have separate vaults.

flashcards.q: What is config drift and why is it dangerous?
flashcards.a: Environments slowly moving apart, so that tests on staging no longer show how prod behaves.
flashcards.more: Causes include hand edits on a server, different database versions, and if (prod) in the code. To prevent it: use the same image, change config through code review, and detect missing required env variables at startup.

flashcards.q: How can staging run the real SMS-sending code without texting customers?
flashcards.a: Use the same gateway class everywhere and give staging the SMS provider's sandbox URL through an env variable.
flashcards.more: An `if (prod)` that skips sending means the real path is never tested before prod. With a sandbox URL in the staging env, the same code runs, the provider accepts the request, and no customer gets a text. Only dev swaps in a log gateway, from one visible place in config.

flashcards.q: What is a business rule?
flashcards.a: A business decision that ends up in code, such as who gets how much discount or which orders are held back.
flashcards.more: The rate chart and the procedure for collecting fees are different things: the chart changes, the procedure doesn't. Some rules are like the chart (numbers, lists); others are like the procedure (complex calculations).

flashcards.q: When is it reasonable to keep a rule in data rather than code?
flashcards.a: When it changes often, business staff change it, it is simple, and a mistake costs little.
flashcards.more: The four questions: how often it changes, who changes it, what a mistake costs, and how complex it is. A discount percentage or a delivery area is a good candidate for data; tax calculation or a balance update is not.

flashcards.q: Which rules are better left in code?
flashcards.a: Risky ones (money, law, security), complex ones (branches, loops, state), and ones that rarely change.
flashcards.more: Put a rule in data and you must build the safety of code review, tests and versioning yourself. For a rarely changed rule that effort never pays off. A complex rule in data slowly turns into an untested programming language.

flashcards.q: What is Symfony ExpressionLanguage used for?
flashcards.a: Running a condition stored as a string (cart.total >= 5000) in a safe, limited language to get a result.
flashcards.more: `$language->evaluate($expr, ['cart' => $cart])` runs the condition, and `lint()` checks the syntax before you save. A condition is really code, so limit who may change it and never run user input through it.

flashcards.q: Why pass a small facts DTO to a rule instead of a Doctrine entity?
flashcards.a: So the rule sees only what it needs, can't call other methods, and stored rules don't break when the entity changes.
flashcards.more: Stored rules sit in the database for a long time. If they depend on deep calls like `cart.getUser().getOrders()`, any change to the entity breaks them. A facts DTO is a stable contract.

flashcards.q: What are the safe steps for changing a rule stored in data?
flashcards.a: Write a new version, test it, dry-run it on old orders, get approval, go live on a date, and record the version on the order.
flashcards.more: Never delete old versions: then you can audit and you can go back. A dry run shows how much discount the rule would suddenly give. With the version on the order, you can answer "why this discount?".

flashcards.q: What does a dry run of a changed rule tell you?
flashcards.a: It replays real past orders (say the last 30 days) with the new rule and shows how many orders and how much money would change.
flashcards.more: It catches the rule that suddenly gives everyone a discount, before a single customer sees it. Example-based tests prove the rule is written correctly; a dry run proves it behaves sensibly on real data.

flashcards.q: How do you stop a rule typo from causing big damage?
flashcards.a: Keep a hard limit in code, such as min($percent, 30), and validate and lint when saving to the data.
flashcards.more: Whatever is written in the data, the code's limit holds. Log and alert when it is exceeded, so a mistake on the admin page is caught before the damage. Numbers in data, limits in code.
